title: Sita's argument
hook: Rama asks Sita to stay behind, and she makes her case

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's calm, toward blame. Don't blame Kaikeyi, he said; this is daiva. Did you fix something before looking for whose fault it was? A new week begins, and Sita speaks. Day five hundred twenty-six.

If you only know Sita from a calendar picture, you may think of her as quiet: eyes lowered, hands folded, walking a step behind. Valmiki's Sita is many things, and quiet isn't the first one that comes to mind in this scene. Rama comes home with his news, and he has a plan for her. She's going to stay in Ayodhya. He's thought it through. And Sita listens to the whole plan, and then takes it apart.
screen: `THE CALENDAR PICTURE.` → `VALMIKI'S SITA.` → `SHE TAKES THE PLAN APART.`

segments.voice: Sita has been waiting at home for the procession. She sees Rama come in alone, pale, with no royal umbrella and no music, and she knows something is wrong. He tells her everything. Then he gives her instructions. Stay here. Serve my father and my mothers. Don't praise me in front of Bharata, because men in power don't like hearing others praised. Keep your vows, live simply, and wait for me. Valmiki says Sita answers out of love and anger together. Her first point is sharp. Father, mother, brother, son, each lives out their own fortune, she says. But a wife shares her husband's. If you've been sent to the forest, so have I. Her second point is practical. If you go into the forest today, I'll walk ahead of you, trampling the thorns and the sharp grass so your path is easier. Her third point is about what she wants. She'd rather be in the forest with him than in a palace without him. She's not asking for permission to suffer. She's describing the forest as a place she wants to see: the mountains, the lakes, the lotus ponds, the birds. She'll be happy there, she says, as long as he's there. Notice the shape of it. Rama made a decision for both of them, kindly and alone. Sita refuses to be decided for. This is the argument many families remember and retell. Valmiki gives her the room to make it, at length, in her own voice, and she isn't finished yet.
screen: `NO UMBRELLA, NO MUSIC.` · `RAMA'S PLAN: STAY HERE.` · `A WIFE SHARES HER HUSBAND'S FORTUNE.` · `I'LL WALK AHEAD, TRAMPLING THORNS.` · then, large: `SITA REFUSES TO BE DECIDED FOR.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Think of a decision someone made for you, out of kindness, without asking. Notice how that felt. Now think of one you've made for someone else the same way. Let both sit side by side. On each breath out, imagine handing the question back to the other person, open, so they can answer it in their own voice. The bell holds the time.
Sita's argument. Asked to stay behind, she answers out of love and anger: a wife shares her husband's fortune, and she'll walk ahead of him through the thorns.
Your line: Sita's argument. Today, before you decide something for someone you love, ask them what they want. Day five hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: In Hindu homes Sita is honored as Rama's devoted companion, and this scene, where she insists on sharing his exile, is often read as her own choice, made in her own voice.

fork.setup: you're Sita. your husband, kindly, has decided you'll stay in the palace while he goes into exile. what do you say?
options: if you're sent to the forest, so am I.
fork.reveal: she argues that a wife shares her husband's fortune, and that she'll walk ahead of him through the thorns.

original.note: Sanskrit sītā: a furrow. her name recalls how Janaka found her in a plowed field.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sita simply followed Rama.
what it means: Rama tells her to stay, and she argues him out of it.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki gives Sita several sargas of her own speech here, one of the longest stretches of a woman's voice in the epic.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 26 (Rama tells Sita; asks her to stay)
Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 27 (Sita's reply: a wife shares her husband's fortune; walking ahead through thorns)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm.
'Love and anger together' renders praṇayakopa or similar in the text; confirm.
Trapdoor claim 'one of the longest stretches of a woman's voice in the epic' is a reading, not a count; a Keeper may soften it.
Sita's name from sītā, furrow: standard; her finding in the field is told in the Bala Kanda.
